source_text:
ἀλλὰ μὲν ἴσως ταῦτα γελάσεις, ὡς αὐτόχρημα τὸ
σοφιστικὸν ἐπανθεῖ αὐτοῖς, καί με τυχὸν ὡς ἐν ὀνείδει καλέσειας σοφιστήν· ἐγὼ δὲ

τὰ καλὰ μὴ θαυμάζειν οὐκ ἔχω, κἂν σιωπήσῃς, ὦ λῷστε, τἀναντία φθεγγόμεθα·
ἀλλὰ μή μοι διδόναι πρᾶγμα ζητοῦντι τὴν ἐκ τῆς σιωπῆς λύπην παραστῆσαι τοῖς
γράμμασιν.
thought_title: Do not make me write out the grief of silence
orientation: Procopius is closing his letter, anticipating that the recipient may mock his praise as sophistry and asking him not to force him to put the pain of silence into writing.
pass_a_gloss: But perhaps you will laugh at these things, because sheer sophistry blooms in them, and perhaps you would call me, as in reproach, a sophist; but I am not able not to admire beautiful things, even if you are silent, best of men, we say opposite things; but do not give me trouble, as I seek to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.

choices.why: αὐτόχρημα means 'the very thing itself,' so 'sheer sophistry' captures the emphatic quality without adding a noun.
ὄνειδος is reproach or insult; the phrase marks the manner of the naming.

choices.term: τὰ καλὰ μὴ θαυμάζειν οὐκ ἔχω
choices.english: I am not able not to admire beautiful things
choices.why: The double negative is emphatic in Greek; keeping both negatives preserves the force.
rejected: I cannot help admiring beautiful things
I cannot but admire what is beautiful

choices.why: λῷστος is a warm vocative address; 'best of men' keeps the direct address.
The verb φθέγγομαι means to utter or speak; 'we say opposite things' is literal and keeps the plural.
πρᾶγμα here means a troublesome task or burden; 'trouble' fits the request not to impose it.

pass_b_english: But perhaps you will laugh at this, since sheer sophistry blooms all over it, and you might even call me a sophist as a reproach. Yet I am not able not to admire beautiful things. Even if you fall silent, best of men, we speak opposite things. But do not give me trouble, as I seek to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.

problems.quote: Do not give me trouble, when I am seeking to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.
problems.source_quote: ἀλλὰ μή μοι διδόναι πρᾶγμα ζητοῦντι τὴν ἐκ τῆς σιωπῆς λύπην παραστῆσαι τοῖς γράμμασιν
problems.why: Source is a wish: 'do not give me trouble seeking...' = 'do not make me present grief in writing.' English reads as a command not to give trouble while he seeks to present grief.
problems.fix: But do not give me trouble, seeking to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.
problems.ruling: Greek infinitive διδόναι with μή expresses wish/prohibition, not command; 'do not make me' required, not 'do not give me trouble when'

problems.why: 'κἂν' is concessive 'even if,' not simple conditional 'if'; the force of 'even should you fall silent' is lost, weakening the rhetorical contrast.
problems.fix: Even if you fall silent, best of men, we speak at cross purposes.
problems.ruling: κἂν σιωπήσῃς is concessive 'even if you are silent'; rendering as simple 'if' loses the concessive force.

edits.old: If you are silent, best of men, we say opposite things.
edits.new: Even if you fall silent, best of men, we speak at cross purposes.

edits.old: Do not give me trouble, when I am seeking to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.
edits.new: But do not give me trouble, seeking to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.

fixed: Changed 'If you are silent' to 'Even if you fall silent' to restore concessive force.
Changed 'Do not give me trouble, when I am seeking' to 'But do not give me trouble, seeking' to restore the wish construction.

problems.why: 'We speak opposite things' means Procopius contradicts himself, not mutual misunderstanding.
problems.fix: I speak against myself; I contradict myself.

problems.quote: do not give me trouble, seeking to present
problems.source_quote: μή μοι διδόναι πρᾶγμα ζητοῦντι τὴν ἐκ τῆς σιωπῆς λύπην παραστῆσαι τοῖς γράμμασιν
problems.why: Procopius asks recipient not to make him seek to depict grief; English makes recipient the seeker.
problems.fix: do not give me trouble by making me seek to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.
problems.ruling: ζητοῦντι is dative agreeing with μοι: 'me seeking to present grief in writing.' English 'seeking' wrongly attaches to recipient as subject.

edits.old: Even if you fall silent, best of men, we speak at cross purposes.
edits.new: Even if you fall silent, best of men, I contradict myself.

edits.old: But do not give me trouble, seeking to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.
edits.new: But do not give me trouble by making me seek to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.

fixed: Changed 'we speak at cross purposes' to 'I contradict myself' to reflect that Procopius speaks opposite things, not mutual misunderstanding.
Changed 'do not give me trouble, seeking to present' to 'do not give me trouble by making me seek to present' to restore Procopius as the one who would seek to depict the grief.

problems.why: 'We speak opposite things' means Procopius and recipient disagree, not self-contradiction.
problems.fix: we speak opposite things, or: we are at odds

problems.quote: by making me seek to present
problems.why: ζητοῦντι is dative participle modifying 'me' (the one seeking), not 'making me seek'.
problems.fix: do not give me, who seek to present, trouble; or: do not trouble me as I seek to present
problems.ruling: ζητοῦντι is dative participle modifying 'me' (the one seeking), not 'making me seek'.

edits.old: Even if you fall silent, best of men, I contradict myself.
edits.new: Even if you fall silent, best of men, we speak opposite things.

edits.old: But do not give me trouble by making me seek to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.
edits.new: But do not give me trouble, as I seek to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.

fixed: Changed 'I contradict myself' to 'we speak opposite things' to reflect the plural subject and disagreement between Procopius and the recipient.
Changed 'by making me seek' to 'as I seek' to reflect the dative participle modifying 'me' rather than causation.

last_rejected.quote: since sheer sophistry blooms all over it
last_rejected.source_quote: ὡς αὐτόχρημα τὸ σοφιστικὸν ἐπανθεῖ αὐτοῖς
last_rejected.why: αὐτοῖς refers to 'these things' (ταῦτα), not 'it'; rendered as if referring to the letter.
last_rejected.fix: since sheer sophistry blooms over these things
last_rejected.ruling: αὐτοῖς refers back to ταῦτα ('these things'), and 'it' in English naturally refers to 'this' (the preceding matter); no meaning changed.

last_rejected.why: 'We speak opposite things' is nonsensical; context demands 'I speak contrary things' (despite σιωπήσῃς, the speaker is Procopius alone).
last_rejected.fix: I speak things that contradict myself.
last_rejected.ruling: φθεγγόμεθα is 1st plural; 'we speak' is literal. Speaker self-inclusiveness is interpretive, not a translation error.

last_rejected.quote: do not give me trouble, as I seek
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀλλὰ μή μοι διδόναι πρᾶγμα ζητοῦντι
last_rejected.why: Infinitive διδόναι with μή is a prohibition: 'do not give me trouble'; but ζητοῦντι is causal/conditional 'since/as I seek,' not temporal 'as I seek.' The force is 'don't make me, who am trying to...'
last_rejected.fix: But do not give me trouble, one who seeks to present in writing the grief that comes from silence.
last_rejected.ruling: 'as I seek' adequately renders ζητοῦντι; causal/conditional nuance is preserved without misleading the reader.
